facts.text: Star Cynthia Rothrock really is a martial arts teacher type: she holds a 7th-degree black belt in Tang Soo Do plus black sashes in Eagle Claw, Northern Shaolin, Pai Lum and Wushu.
Doug Wright, who plays the class slacker Termite, also appeared in the splatter-comedy The Toxic Avenger Part II (1989).
Cynthia Rothrock took this film partly to dodge another Golden Harvest job: rappelling off Hong Kong's tallest building with no safety net. She was happy to trade it for Utah.
Star Cynthia Rothrock is said to be the inspiration for Sonya Blade, the fighter from the video game Mortal Kombat.
The song playing, "Distant Storm," is sung by a young Tori Amos. She didn't want her name on it, so the credit goes to an invented band called Tess Makes Good.
Tori Amos was paid just $150 to record "Distant Storm." She only learned it was in this movie in 1993, when fanzine founder Tom Richards recognized her voice and played it to her.
China O'Brien skipped theaters in the US and went straight to video in 1990.
Stars Cynthia Rothrock and Richard Norton hated their performances in this first meeting of China and Matt. At the first screening the film tape tore and skipped the scene, to their relief.
Film scholar Rikke Schubart says producers made China the daughter of a slain cop and paired her with ex-boyfriend Matt to make star Cynthia Rothrock seem more feminine and less threatening.
The story is a gender-swapped riff on Walking Tall (1973), the film inspired by real Tennessee sheriff Buford Pusser, per Den of Geek: a lawman's kin takes on a corrupt small town.
The "guy with the funny hand" is real: Keith Cooke (Dakota) broke his hand luging with Cynthia Rothrock before filming, so the injury was written into his character. He leaned on kicks.
Richard Norton (Matt Conroy) made his screen debut in The Octagon (1980). Fighting Stars magazine ranked his finale there against Chuck Norris #13 on its list of the 25 greatest fight scenes.
Beaver Creek, Utah is fictional. The film was shot around Park City, Heber City, Kamas and Coalville, Utah.
The story was conceived by Sandra Weintraub, daughter of producer Fred Weintraub (Enter the Dragon). Director Robert Clouse wrote the script and directed it.
Goof alert: in the sawmill brawl, after a thug waves a chainsaw, a stunt man is wire-yanked backward. A blue safety mat is faintly visible under the sawdust where he lands.
Director Robert Clouse made Bruce Lee's Enter the Dragon (1973), the film that also reunited Golden Harvest collaborators on this production.
China O'Brien and its sequel were reportedly shot together in about six weeks. Star Cynthia Rothrock's Hong Kong films took months, with weeks spent on single fight scenes.
China O'Brien is the only movie in which star Cynthia Rothrock ever broke a bone while filming. It was a finger.
Golden Harvest boss Raymond Chow wanted to break Cynthia Rothrock out to Western audiences, so the Hong Kong studio made this film in America as her lead vehicle.
Both films were shot out of order. When newcomer Cynthia Rothrock asked director Robert Clouse for a scene's context, he said, "Doesn't matter! Just do it!"
The parade where China rides a car to promote her sheriff run was filmed at a real Utah parade. Nobody was told, and a local radio station reported her fictional campaign as fact.
Producer Fred Weintraub said in a 1993 documentary that the world was "ready for a female action hero."
Cinematographer Kent L. Wakeford shot Martin Scorsese's Mean Streets (1973) and Alice Doesn't Live Here Anymore (1974) before lensing this Utah kung-fu sheriff story.
Richard Norton (Matt Conroy) was once considered for the role of Martin Riggs in Lethal Weapon, the part that went to Mel Gibson.
Production paused when Cynthia Rothrock had to fly back to Hong Kong to reshoot the ending of her film Righting Wrongs after the original cut got a bad reception in Taiwan.
Cynthia Rothrock says director Robert Clouse sometimes fed lines off-camera for actors to repeat. In one scene with Richard Norton, they delivered dialogue staring ahead with the sun in their eyes.
Keith Cooke (Dakota) later auditioned for Liu Kang in Mortal Kombat (1995) but was cast as the ninja Reptile instead.
The script never suggested a romance between China and Matt. Cynthia Rothrock says she and Richard Norton chose to imply one in their performances, helped by their real-life friendship.
Keith Cooke was born Keith Hirabayashi. Producer Fred Weintraub advised him to use his mother's surname Cooke, to sound more native American.
Cynthia Rothrock tore the ACL in her right knee in the 1980s and skipped surgery. Doctors found her quadriceps and hamstrings were strong enough to hold her kneecap in place.
China O'Brien II was shot right after this film, before it was released. Billy Blanks has a cameo in the sequel.
Cynthia Rothrock told Daily Grindhouse she'd love to remake China O'Brien today, darker and grittier, though she credits the original with "fantastic energy."
After Bruce Lee's death, director Robert Clouse completed Lee's unfinished Game of Death (1978) with a new storyline and cast.
Variety called China O'Brien "an okay showcase" for Cynthia Rothrock.
On video, China O'Brien reportedly sold 20,000 units in its first month, a strong result for a low-budget movie with no name stars, according to Den of Geek.
Cynthia Rothrock has complained that the poster art for this film and its sequel mis-sold it: the woman pictured is clearly not her, and lacks her muscular build.
Richard Norton (Matt Conroy) was a bodyguard for Rod Stewart, David Bowie and Fleetwood Mac before acting. He later appeared in Mad Max: Fury Road (2015).
The film is name-checked in the 2019 documentary In Search of the Last Action Heroes, which features star Cynthia Rothrock.
Cynthia Rothrock says she was "lucky" Golden Harvest made her a lead in China O'Brien. Producers felt her films earned money, which got her the lead in Lady Dragon next.
Cynthia Rothrock and Richard Norton co-starred in five films in the 1990s: both China O'Brien movies, Lady Dragon, Rage and Honor and Rage and Honor II.
